content: The phenomenon of male lactation in humans has become increasingly observed in recent years, primarily due to the use of medications that stimulate the mammary glands in men. While it is widely known that males have nipples, many are unaware that they also possess mammary glands. Typically, the amount of mammary tissue in males is minimal and not noticeable. However, when male breast tissue becomes visibly developed, this condition is referred to as gynecomastia. Under the influence of specific hormonal stimuli—similar to those experienced by females during pregnancy and childbirth—the mammary glands in males are capable of producing milk. However, the quantity of milk produced by males is significantly lower compared to that of lactating females. Interestingly, male lactation can sometimes occur without the use of hormonal treatments. For example, newborn baby boys (and girls) may occasionally produce milk due to the high levels of maternal hormones they are exposed to during pregnancy and childbirth. This phenomenon is known as witch's milk. Male lactation is most commonly associated with hormonal treatments administered to men undergoing therapy for prostate cancer. In such cases, female hormones are used to slow the growth of cancerous prostate tissue, but these same hormones can also stimulate the mammary glands, leading to lactation. Additionally, male-to-female transgender individuals may experience lactation as a result of the hormonal regimens they take to facilitate their physical transition. In some cases, male lactation can occur as a side effect of certain medications, such as antipsychotic drugs. Extreme stress, combined with intense physical exertion and malnutrition, has also been documented as a cause of male lactation. This phenomenon was first studied in survivors of Nazi concentration camps who were liberated after World War II. Similarly, some American prisoners of war (POWs) returning from the Korean and Vietnam Wars reported experiencing male lactation. It is also possible for males (and females) to induce lactation through consistent stimulation of the nipples, such as through massage or simulated sucking, over an extended period of time, often requiring months of effort. Male lactation is not exclusive to humans and has been observed in certain non-human species. For instance, the Dayak fruit bat (Dyacopterus spadiceus) is known to exhibit male lactation, with lactating males potentially assisting in the nursing of their offspring. Male goats have also been reported to lactate on occasion. Spontaneous male lactation and even instances of nursing have occasionally been documented in humans. In his book Why Is Sex Fun?, Jared Diamond describes cases of male and female cancer patients treated with estrogen who began to lactate after being injected with prolactin. He also suggests that mechanical stimulation of male nipples could lead to lactation by triggering the release of prolactin. Furthermore, there have been reports of teenage boys experiencing lactation after self-stimulation of their nipples.
